details:
**Bodhi tree**
The fig tree at Bodh Gaya in northeastern India under which Siddhartha meditated until he attained enlightenment and became the Buddha ("awakened one"). Accounts say he then spent seven weeks (49 days) in its vicinity; during one of those weeks a storm arose and the serpent king Mucalinda coiled around him and spread his hoods over him as shelter.

**Four Sights**
On trips outside the palace where he had been shielded from all suffering, Prince Siddhartha saw an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and finally a wandering ascetic (holy man). The first three revealed the reality of suffering, and the fourth inspired him to renounce his royal life to seek a way out of it.

**Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path**
The core of the Buddha's teaching: life is marked by suffering (dukkha), suffering arises from craving, suffering can end (nirvana), and the way to end it is the Noble Eightfold Path. The path consists of right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, and concentration.

**Deer Park at Sarnath**
The park near Benares (Varanasi) where the Buddha gave his first sermon after his enlightenment to five former ascetic companions, an event called "setting in motion the wheel of the Dharma." In it he taught the Four Noble Truths, the Eightfold Path, and the Middle Way.

**Queen Maya's white elephant dream**
The night the Buddha was conceived, his mother, Queen Maha Maya, dreamed that a white elephant with six tusks entered her right side. This was interpreted as a sign that she would bear a great being.

**Mara and the earth-touching mudra**
As Siddhartha sat beneath the Bodhi tree, the demon Mara attacked him with armies and sent his daughters to tempt him. When Mara challenged his right to the seat of enlightenment, Siddhartha touched the ground with his right hand and the earth bore witness for him; this bhumisparsha ("earth-touching") mudra is the most common gesture in Buddha images.

**Middle Way**
The Buddha's teaching that the path to liberation lies between the extremes of luxurious indulgence, which he knew as a prince, and harsh self-mortification, which he practiced for six years as an ascetic. He realized this after nearly starving himself to death.

**Siddhartha Gautama, prince of the Shakyas**
The Buddha's birth name. He was a Kshatriya prince of the Shakya clan, hence the title Shakyamuni ("sage of the Shakyas"), born at Lumbini and raised in Kapilavastu by his father, King Suddhodana. The seer Asita predicted he would become either a universal monarch or a great spiritual teacher, so his father kept him confined within the palace.

**The Great Departure: Rahula, Kanthaka, and Channa**
When his son was born, Siddhartha named him Rahula ("fetter"), seeing the child as a new bond tying him to worldly life. He soon left his wife Yashodhara and son at night, riding his horse Kanthaka with his charioteer Channa, to become a wandering ascetic.

**Cunda's last meal and Sujata's milk-rice**
Just before his enlightenment, the young woman Sujata offered the starving Siddhartha a bowl of milk-rice (rice pudding), which ended his period of extreme fasting. Decades later, his final meal came from the blacksmith Cunda (Kunda), either spoiled pork or mushrooms; it made him gravely ill, and he soon died and entered parinirvana at Kushinagar.

**Flower Sermon**
A story in which the Buddha, instead of speaking, silently held up a flower, and only his disciple Mahakashyapa understood and smiled. It is regarded as the origin of Zen (Chan) Buddhism's tradition of wordless, mind-to-mind transmission.

**Bamiyan Buddhas and other famous statues**
Two giant Buddhas carved into a cliff in Afghanistan's Bamiyan valley, the larger about 180 feet tall, were dynamited by the Taliban in 2001. Other famous examples include the bronze Daibutsu ("Great Buddha") at Todai-ji in Nara, Japan; the rock-cut statues of China's Yungang Grottoes and the Mogao Caves ("Caves of the Thousand Buddhas"); a Buddha head enclosed in tree roots at Wat Mahathat (the Temple of the Great Relic) in Ayutthaya, Thailand; and a monolithic statue in Hussain Sagar lake in Hyderabad.

**Gandharan art, relics, and stupas**
The gold Bimaran casket, a reliquary from Gandhara in Afghanistan, shows the Buddha in a Greco-Roman influenced style and is among the earliest images of him. Legend says the Buddha showed the shape of a stupa (relic mound) by turning his alms bowl upside down; the Temple of the Tooth in Kandy, Sri Lanka, houses his tooth relic, and symbols of his footprints are often marked with wheels.

**Parable of the poisoned arrow and the 84th problem**
The Buddha compared someone who demands answers to metaphysical questions before practicing to a man shot by a poisoned arrow who will not let the surgeon remove it until he learns who shot it. In another story, he told a farmer that everyone has 83 problems he cannot fix, but he can help with the 84th: the wish to have no problems.

**Angulimala**
A brigand who killed people and wore their fingers as a garland, supposedly to collect a thousand fingers as a fee demanded by his teacher. The Buddha calmly confronted and converted him, and Angulimala became a monk; the Buddha similarly tamed the demon Alavaka.
